proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 20 currently gives Vendor a broad indemnity from us and gives us none, which is a walk-away position for us: we need Vendor to defend third-party IP infringement claims and claims arising from its breach of law, data breaches it causes, and its gross negligence or wilful misconduct. We have added the customary notice/control/cooperation procedure, the usual infringement exclusions and procure/modify/replace/refund remedies (which Section 9.3 already assumes exist at Section 20.5), and narrowed our own indemnity to Customer-provided content and our breach of law.

ops.newText: 20.1 Vendor shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; (c) any unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct.
ops.oldText: 20.1 Customer shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Vendor from every claim relating in any way to Customer's use of the Services.

ops.text: 20.2 Customer shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Vendor from and against third-party claims to the extent arising out of content or materials Customer provides to Vendor or Customer's breach of Applicable Law. 20.3 The indemnified Party shall give the indemnifying Party prompt written notice of the claim; the indemnifying Party will have control of the defence and settlement, provided that no settlement admitting liability or imposing an obligation on the indemnified Party is made without its prior written consent; and the indemnified Party will provide reasonable cooperation at the indemnifying Party's expense and may participate with its own counsel at its own cost. 20.4 Vendor's obligation under Section 20.1(a) does not apply to the extent a claim arises from Customer's unauthorized modification of the Services or Deliverables, their combination with items not supplied or recommended by Vendor, or Vendor's compliance with Customer's written specifications. 20.5 For a claim under Section 20.1(a), Vendor shall at its expense procure the rights necessary for Customer to continue using the affected item or modify or replace it with a functionally equivalent non-infringing item; if neither is reasonably achievable, Customer may terminate the affected Services or Deliverable and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees and Fees paid for the affected item.

proposal.summary: Replace one-way Customer indemnity with a Vendor indemnity (IP, law, data breach, wilful misconduct), add standard procedure, exclusions and IP remedies, and narrow Customer's indemnity.

quote: 20. INDEMNIFICATION 20.1 Customer shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Vendor from every claim relating in any way to Customer's use of the Services.
rationale: Section 20 is a one-way indemnity: Customer indemnifies Vendor for "every claim relating in any way to Customer's use of the Services", and no Vendor indemnity exists anywhere in the Agreement (a search for indemnity language returns only Section 20.1, the Section 19.4 remedies carve-out, the Section 21.3 Excluded Claims definition, and Section 30.5). There is therefore no Vendor IP infringement indemnity, and Section 9.3's termination right expressly depends on "the remedies required by Section 20.5", which does not exist. That is walk-away territory under the rule (no Vendor IP indemnity plus a one-way Customer indemnity), so it fails the fallback on a material term. Our redline inserts the preferred Vendor indemnity (IP infringement, breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused Customer Data incidents, gross negligence/wilful misconduct), adds standard notice/control/cooperation procedure, the customary modification/combination/specification exclusions and procure-modify-replace-refund remedies at Section 20.5 (curing the broken cross-reference), and narrows Customer's indemnity to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of Applicable Law.

quote: 14.2 Upon creation and subject to payment of the applicable Fees, Customer owns each Deliverable created specifically for Customer. Vendor hereby assigns to Customer all worldwide right, title, and interest in those Deliverables and shall obtain equivalent assignments from its personnel.
rationale: The IP scheme meets the preferred position in full. § 14.1 confirms Customer owns Customer Data, Customer Confidential Information and its independent IP, with no transfer to Vendor beyond a processing right limited to delivering the Services (reinforced by § 15.1's no-sale/no-model-training restrictions). § 14.2 gives Customer ownership of each Deliverable with a present assignment from Vendor plus personnel assignments and further-assurance. § 14.3 lets Vendor retain only Vendor Technology and channels any embedded Vendor Technology into the § 13.2 licence, which is perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free and fully paid, extends to Affiliates and contractors, and includes modification and derivative works. § 14.4 negates joint ownership absent a signed instrument and keeps feedback voluntary with Customer retaining unrestricted use. No assignment of Customer IP or data to Vendor and no joint-ownership trap, so no redline is warranted.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have moved the mutual cap to the greater of twelve months' Fees or USD 1,000,000, as a one-month cap is far below a meaningful recovery for a USD 2,000,000 per year commitment. We also removed "without exception" so that the Excluded Claims regime in Sections 21.2 and 21.3 (indemnities, confidentiality, data protection and security, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement) sits outside the cap as drafted.

ops.newText: Except for Excluded Claims, which are not subject to any limitation of liability, each Party's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of (a) the Fees paid or payable by Customer under this Agreement in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim and (b) USD 1,000,000.
ops.oldText: Each Party's aggregate liability shall not exceed Fees actually paid in the one month preceding the event, without exception.

proposal.summary: Raise the mutual liability cap to the greater of 12 months' Fees or USD 1,000,000 and preserve the Excluded Claims carve-outs.

quote: 21.1 Each Party's aggregate liability shall not exceed Fees actually paid in the one month preceding the event, without exception.
rationale: Section 21.1 caps each Party at only one month of Fees actually paid — well below the fallback of 12 months' fees and inside walk-away territory (a cap below six months' fees). The phrase "without exception" also overrides the otherwise sound Excluded Claims regime in 21.2/21.3, pulling indemnification, confidentiality, data-protection/security, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement inside a one-month cap with no super-cap. The cap is mutual and 21.3 correctly excludes Customer's payment obligations from "damages", so the minimal edit is to reset the basis to the greater of 12 months' Fees paid or payable and USD 1,000,000 and delete "without exception" so the existing carve-outs operate.
ruleTitle: Limitation of liability — cap, mutuality and carve-outs

quote: 24.1 Customer may assign this Agreement or an Order Form without Vendor's consent to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets or business to which the Agreement relates.
rationale: Section 24 meets the preferred position in full: 24.1 lets Customer assign to an Affiliate or M&A successor without Vendor consent (notice only); 24.2 restricts Vendor assignment, delegation and transfer by change of control to Customer's consent (not unreasonably withheld) and bars assignment to a Customer competitor; 24.3 applies a mutual reasonable-consent standard to other assignments; and 24.4 expressly denies Vendor any right to terminate, suspend, reprice, accelerate Fees or reduce service on Customer's change of control. Section 13.3 aligns licence transfers with permitted Section 24 assignments, and no other provision (including the insolvency termination right in 9.2, which carves out lawful reorganizations) creates a change-of-control exit or re-pricing right against us. No redline needed.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have deleted the sole-and-exclusive-provider commitment in Section 2.2: our playbook does not permit exclusivity or sole-supplier obligations on us, and full-term exclusivity with no performance-based exit is not acceptable. This also removes a direct conflict with Section 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges we have made no exclusivity commitment. If Vendor needs some protection, we could consider exclusivity limited to hosted analytics services for 12 months, terminating automatically if Vendor misses service levels or delivery dates.

quote: 2.2 Vendor will be Customer's sole and exclusive provider of hosted analytics services throughout the term.
rationale: Section 2.2 imposes exclusivity on us (Customer) by naming Vendor our sole and exclusive provider of hosted analytics services "throughout the term" — exclusive dealing for the full term with no performance-based exit, which is walk-away territory under this rule and fails the fallback (category-limited, 12 months, automatic termination on missed service levels or delivery dates). It also contradicts Section 12.3, where Vendor acknowledges we have made no exclusivity commitment. Smallest edit to the preferred position is deletion of the clause; the fallback (12-month, category-limited exclusivity with a performance exit) is offered in the comment as a compromise. The take-or-pay minimum in Section 2.1 is a separate commercial term addressed under its own rule.

quote: 9.4 Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience, in whole or in part, upon thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor. Customer owes Fees only for conforming Services provided through the effective termination date, and Vendor shall promptly refund prepaid Fees allocable to the period after that date.
rationale: Searches for "liquidated damages", "penalty", "early termination", "termination fee", "shortfall" and "minimum" return no provision requiring Customer to pay liquidated damages, a penalty, or a minimum/early-termination charge. This meets the preferred position (no Customer-payable liquidated damages or penalties). On the contrary, § 9.4 lets Customer terminate for convenience owing only Fees for conforming Services delivered, with refund of prepaid Fees; § 7.1 bars unidentified minimum-use charges; and § 27.3 allows force-majeure termination "without penalty". The § 2.1 take-or-pay commitment is a volume commitment rather than a liquidated-damages or penalty mechanic and is assessed under the minimum-commitment rule, so it is not flagged here to avoid double-counting the same commercial term.

This aligns § 13.1 with §§ 13.2-13.3 and our playbook position that the licence cover Affiliates and contractors and not be revocable at will.

ops.oldText: Vendor grants Customer alone a non-transferable licence, revocable at Vendor's sole discretion, to use the Services without Affiliates or contractors.

quote: 13.1 Vendor grants Customer alone a non-transferable licence, revocable at Vendor's sole discretion, to use the Services without Affiliates or contractors.
rationale: § 13.1 is the operative Services licence grant and fails the fallback on two material terms: it expressly excludes Affiliates and contractors with no path to add them (walk-away territory under the rule), and it is revocable at Vendor's sole discretion. § 13.2 cures neither point because it is limited to paid-up/embedded software and Vendor Technology, not the Services. § 13.3 helps on revocation (notice-and-cure only) and on transfer to an Affiliate or successor, but it addresses assignment of licence rights rather than day-to-day Affiliate and contractor use, and it directly conflicts with § 13.1's "revocable at Vendor's sole discretion". The redline makes the minimal edit to reach the preferred position by extending the grant to Affiliates and contractors acting on our behalf and tying revocation and transfer to the standard already agreed in § 13.3.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We cannot accept restrictions on the products or services we may develop, buy or sell, so we have deleted § 12.4 — a 24-month post-term, worldwide, undefined-scope non-compete is outside our playbook and also directly contradicts § 12.3, which confirms we have given no non-compete commitment. If the relationship genuinely needs protection, we could discuss a restriction limited to a single named competing product, during the term only and no more than 12 months, with carve-outs for internal development and acquisitions.
proposal.summary: Delete the 24-month worldwide non-compete binding Customer in § 12.4.

quote: 12.4 During the term and for twenty-four months thereafter, Customer shall not develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory.
rationale: § 12.4 binds Customer (our party) with a post-term non-compete of twenty-four months, worldwide ("in any territory"), covering any product or service that "competes with Vendor" — undefined scope with no carve-out for internal development or acquisitions (indeed it expressly bars acquisitions). That is squarely in walk-away territory under NONCOMPETE (post-term restriction longer than 12 months and undefined scope), so it fails both the preferred and the fallback positions. It also directly contradicts § 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges Customer has made no exclusivity or non-compete commitment. The smallest edit that reaches the preferred position is deletion of § 12.4, leaving § 12.3 to govern; we offer the narrowed fallback (single named product, in-term only, ≤12 months, with development and acquisition carve-outs) in the comment. No other provision restricts Customer's business — the only other competition reference (§ 24.2) restricts Vendor's assignment and benefits us.

quote: 9.4 Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience, in whole or in part, upon thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor. Customer owes Fees only for conforming Services provided through the effective termination date, and Vendor shall promptly refund prepaid Fees allocable to the period after that date. Vendor has no corresponding convenience-termination right during a committed term.
rationale: Section 9.4 meets the preferred position in full: we may terminate the Agreement or any Order Form for convenience (in whole or in part) on thirty days' written notice, we owe Fees only through the termination date, Vendor must refund prepaid Fees allocable to the post-termination period, and Vendor is expressly denied any convenience-termination right during a committed term. No early-termination fee or penalty appears anywhere (§ 27.3 likewise confirms termination "without penalty"), and no other clause gives Vendor a convenience or change-of-control exit (§ 24.4 bars a Vendor termination right on our change of control). Noting only, without flagging here: the § 2.1 take-or-pay commitment ("without reduction or termination rights") sits in tension with § 9.4's refund/fee-stop mechanics; that is the minimum-commitment term addressed under the MINCOMMIT rule and is not double-flagged under T4C.

quote: 22.1 Vendor may audit Customer's compliance with licence quantities no more than once in any twelve-month period, on at least thirty days' prior written notice, during normal business hours, and in a manner that does not unreasonably disrupt Customer. An audit will be conducted off-site where practicable by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality.
rationale: Section 22 meets the preferred position in every material respect: audits are limited to once in any twelve-month period (§22.1), require at least thirty days' prior written notice, are confined to normal business hours, must be off-site where practicable and conducted by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality. Section 22.2 places audit costs on Vendor unless the audit establishes an underpayment exceeding five percent, and expressly bars Vendor and its auditor from directly accessing Customer systems, unrelated Customer Data, privileged material or another supplier's confidential information — so the walk-away concerns (unlimited/unannounced audits, remote system access) do not arise. Section 22.3 adds customer-favourable protections (findings are Customer Confidential Information, use limited to enforcement, copy of the final report, and finality on payment of a shortfall). Section 23 ("Records and Customer Assurance") contains no substantive paragraphs and adds no further audit or assurance obligations on us. No redline needed.

We have replaced it with transition assistance for up to six months at Vendor's then-current rates; we can accept 90 days as a fallback.

ops.newText: Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement or an Order Form for any reason, Vendor shall, at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six months at Vendor's then-current rates, including export, migration, and knowledge-transfer support. quote: 11.1 Immediately on termination Vendor shall discontinue all assistance and permanently delete Customer Data without offering an export or migration support.
rationale: Sections 11.2 and 11.3 already deliver the data-return and certified-deletion elements of the preferred position (return within 30 days in a commonly used machine-readable format, deletion certified by an officer after Customer confirms return). However, Section 11.1 sits squarely in walk-away territory: it mandates immediate permanent deletion of Customer Data on termination with no export or migration support, and it provides no transition assistance period at all (neither 6 months preferred nor 90 days fallback). It also directly contradicts 11.2/11.3, creating a real risk that Vendor deletes our data before any export. Smallest fix is to replace 11.1 with a six-month transition-assistance obligation at Vendor's then-current rates and subordinate deletion to Sections 11.2 and 11.3; 90 days of assistance is an acceptable fallback.

quote: 19.2 For fifteen days after delivery, each Deliverable will materially conform to its documentation; after that date Vendor has no correction or refund obligation.

The failure is duration: § 19.2 caps the Deliverable conformance warranty at fifteen days after delivery and then states Vendor has "no correction or refund obligation," which overrides the unqualified § 19.1 conformance warranty and guts the § 19.4 remedy. Fifteen days is below the fallback floor (90 days software / 30 days services) and, given the fifteen business day acceptance window in § 6.1, the warranty would expire at or before acceptance testing concludes. Minimal edit extends the period to ninety (90) days and deletes the cut-off sentence, pointing to the existing § 19.4 remedy.
